CARMICHAEL Department of Geophysics, University of Western Ontario, London, Ontario Received February 20, 1973 Revision accepted for publication April 5, 1973 Anorthositic rocks 20 to 30 km south of the Grenville Front in the Grenville Province of Ontario have a stable remanent magnetization which yields a paleomagnetic pole at 161" E, 8" N. This pole is close to other poles from the Precambrian of North America of 1050 m.y. age. Paleomagnetic results have also been obtained from two rock units in the southern part of the Grenville Province of Ontario. These are a pyroxenite exposed near Wilberforce and the Tudor Gabbro exposed near Madoc. The directions of remanent magnetization yield pole positions as follows: Wilberforce pyroxenite-148" E, 14.5" S; Tudor Gabbro-137" E, 17" N. CARMICHAEL Department of Geophysics, University of Western Ontario, London, Ontario Received February 20, 1973 Revision accepted for publication April 5, 1973 Anorthositic rocks 20 to 30 km south of the Grenville Front in the Grenville Province of Ontario have a stable remanent magnetization which yields a paleomagnetic pole at 161" E, 8" N. This pole is close to other poles from the Precambrian of North America of 1050 m.y. age. Paleomagnetic results have also been obtained from two rock units in the southern part of the Grenville Province of Ontario. These are a pyroxenite exposed near Wilberforce and the Tudor Gabbro exposed near Madoc. The directions of remanent magnetization yield pole positions as follows: Wilberforce pyroxenite-148" E, 14.5" S; Tudor Gabbro-137" E, 17" N. These pole positions, together with others from the literature, which have been derived from rock units 200 km or more south of the GrenviUe Front, plot farther west in the Pacific than do poles of inferred similar age from other regions of North America. A possible interpretation of these results is that the southern part of the Grenville province was formed some 30" SE of its present position. Megascopically the St. Charles anorthosite samples are medium-grained, massive, and consist of white feldspar with about 10 to 15% of black ferromagnesian minerals. In thin sec- tion the plagioclase is clear, twinned, and weakly zoned. The dark minerals are amphi- bole and biotite. Accessory minerals include epidote, garnet, and rutile. Opaque oxides are rare; typically only one or two grains are found in any thin section. The samples from the single River Valley anorthosite site are dark gray, massive rocks with the ferromagnesians only slightly darker than the abundant and coarse-grained plagio- clase. In thin section the plagioclase is twinned, inconspicuously zoned, and has a dusty appear- ance in plane polarized light. Clinopyroxene, invariably with coronas of hornblende, forms 15-20% of the rock. Large opaque oxides are notably absent. (1972) and Palmer and Car- michael (1972) to postulate that part of the Grenville Province was once displaced relative to the remainder of the Canadian shield. In this paper we present the data which led us to that conclusion. Because lithological types northwest of the Grenville Front can be traced for some distance into the Grenville Province (100 km in the case of the distinctive iron formations of the Labrador trough) it is clear that the Grenville Front itself does not repre- sent the suture between the two ancient plates. The directions of the two components are chiefly to the northwest, 20" upward (northwest component) and to the east, 65" downward (east component). The northwest direction is thought to be the primary igneous T.R.M. and no reversely magnetized sites with this direction were encountered in the Mealy suite. A test of the reality of this type origin for the volcanic line should give evidence on the Ceno- zoic motion of the African Plate. This first paper of the series describes data from the Haruj Assuad basaltic volcanics of central Libya. During this century, Kanter (1940), Bellair et al. (1952), Klitzsch (in Williams 1966) and Klitzsch ( 1967) have given geological descriptions of this relatively inaccessible area. Klitzsch (1967) gives the most comprehensive account of the area, based on information gathered during oil exploration activities. The 45 000 km2 volcanic area is the largest in North Africa, but is generally of low elevation and relief, suggesting formation by a relatively small number of very fluid pahoehoe basaltic flows. Occasional cones, shield vol- canoes and plugs interrupt the monotonous scenery. The frequent preservation of volcanic landforms suggests a recent termination for volcanic

Klitzsch (1967) gives the most comprehensive account of the area, based on information gathered during oil exploration activities. The 45 000 km2 volcanic area is the largest in North Africa, but is generally of low elevation and relief, suggesting formation by a relatively small number of very fluid pahoehoe basaltic flows. Occasional cones, shield vol- canoes and plugs interrupt the monotonous scenery. The frequent preservation of volcanic landforms suggests a recent termination for volcanic activity in the area. Stratigraphic evi- dence indicates that the age span of volcanic activity is Middle Miocene and younger (i.e. < 18 my). Klitzsch ( 1967) has recognized six major groups of flows of successively younger Pliocene to Holocene age (B1 to B6/7) from the degree of weathering of flow surfaces. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction Considerable amount of paleomagnetic data on rocks of various ages has been obtained from North America and Europe and this has been used in attempting to outline the North Atlantic paleogeography. Since in all such reconstruction models Greenland is considered to have moved as a distinct crustal plate, reliable paleomag- netic data from Greenland are crucial. However, until recently, such data from Greenland have been rather sparse because of inaccessibility and difficulties in sampling. Sequences of basaltic lava flows of Early Tertiary age are exposed on the western and eastern margins of Greenland and these forma- tions together with the lava sequences on Baffin Island of Canada, Faeroes, and the British Isles have been considered as constituents of the Brito-Arctic volcanic province. Tarling (1967) reported the results of the first paleomagnetic study on the East Greenland Tertiary lavas and this was followed by a West Greenland result from lava flows on Ubekendt Ejland (Tarling and Otulana 1972). Since in all such reconstruction models Greenland is considered to have moved as a distinct crustal plate, reliable paleomag- netic data from Greenland are crucial. However, until recently, such data from Greenland have been rather sparse because of inaccessibility and difficulties in sampling. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Master University, Hamilton, Ontario L8S 4Ml The Whitestone anorthosite and diorite are situated in the Grenville Structural Province north of Parry Sound, Ontario. They are intruded into sediments and igneous rocks, the whole being metamorphosed to amphibolite facies. Aside from soft magnetizations due to the present field four magnetizations are present, two owing to hematite, the third mainly to magnetite, and a fourth of uncertain source. It is argued that these are thermoremanent magnetizations acquired during very slow cooling following regional metamorphism in the interval 1100 to 1000 m.y. A single-stage cooling model based on Neel's single domain theory is developed, which suggests that the hematite magnetizations were acquired during slow cooling at about 240 T and the magnetite magnetizations at about 200 T. The poles from Whitestone rocks fall among a group of poles from elsewhere in the Grenville Province. There are serious problems in integrating these Grenville poles with those from other parts of the Canadian Shield, and three possible ways of relating them are evaluated. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction The town of Gowganda is about 190 km north of Sudbury, Ontario (Fig. 1). From 1908 to 1972, native silver was mined near the town from narrow veins in the undulating Nipissing diabase sill. This group con- tains eight reversely and two normally polarized site mean remanence directions. This result con- firms the earlier observation (Symons 1971) that the Earth's magnetic field was dominantly reversed during emplacement and cooling of the Nipissing sills with minor periods of normal polarity. The concordance of these populations leads to three conclusions. First, the Nipissing sills in all five collections have retained a stable primary remanence. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction Paleomagnetism is an important tool for geological correlation of igneous as well as sedimentary rocks. In India such geological correlation has been attempted for dolerite dikes from Gondwana basins of Damodar Valley (Athavale and Verma 1970). Husnain and Qureshy ( 1971 ) have studied several dikes from the southern peninsular shield of India. On the basis of paleomagnetic studies, some of the dikes have been found to be cor- relatable with the Deccan traps. From other countries there are examples of classification of dikes on the basis of paleomagnetic studi

tudies, some of the dikes have been found to be cor- relatable with the Deccan traps. From other countries there are examples of classification of dikes on the basis of paleomagnetic studies, such as Evans (1968) in Australia, Strangway (1965, 1966) and Larson and Strangway (1969) in Canada and the U.S.A. In this paper we report results of paleomagnetic studies of the Newer Dolerites from Singh- bhum, Rihar, India. During the Precambrian there appear to have been three main episodes of dike intru- sion throughout peninsular India (Pascoe 1950, p. 469). The earliest corresponded to the contcmporaneous traps of the Dharwar sys- tem. This was uniformly felt over the whole of peninsular India. The second episode is repre- sented by dikes and sills of the Cuddapah sys- tem. This was recognized mainly in many parts of the southern peninsula but more restrictedly in the northern half. The third one coincided with the outbursts of Malani rhyolites. This is more evident in the northern half of peninsula. The volcanic types of the Dharwar and those of Cuddapah are in most cases sharply con- trasted by the degree of alteration they exhibit. Can. J. Earth Sci., 11,1043-1054 (1974) CAN. J. EARTH SCI. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction Paleomagnetism is an important tool for geological correlation of igneous as well as sedimentary rocks. In India such geological correlation has been attempted for dolerite dikes from Gondwana basins of Damodar Valley (Athavale and Verma 1970). Husnain and Qureshy ( 1971 ) have studied several dikes from the southern peninsular shield of India. On the basis of paleomagnetic studies, some of the dikes have been found to be cor- relatable with the Deccan traps. From other countries there are examples of classification of dikes on the basis of paleomagnetic studi

tudies, some of the dikes have been found to be cor- relatable with the Deccan traps. From other countries there are examples of classification of dikes on the basis of paleomagnetic studies, such as Evans (1968) in Australia, Strangway (1965, 1966) and Larson and Strangway (1969) in Canada and the U.S.A. In this paper we report results of paleomagnetic studies of the Newer Dolerites from Singh- bhum, Rihar, India. During the Precambrian there appear to have been three main episodes of dike intru- sion throughout peninsular India (Pascoe 1950, p. 469). The earliest corresponded to the contcmporaneous traps of the Dharwar sys- tem. This was uniformly felt over the whole of peninsular India. The second episode is repre- sented by dikes and sills of the Cuddapah sys- tem. This was recognized mainly in many parts of the southern peninsula but more restrictedly in the northern half. The third one coincided with the outbursts of Malani rhyolites. This is more evident in the northern half of peninsula. The volcanic types of the Dharwar and those of Cuddapah are in most cases sharply con- trasted by the degree of alteration they exhibit. Can. J. Earth Sci., 11,1043-1054 (1974) CAN. J. EARTH SCI. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction Paleomagnetism is an important tool for geological correlation of igneous as well as sedimentary rocks. In India such geological correlation has been attempted for dolerite dikes from Gondwana basins of Damodar Valley (Athavale and Verma 1970). Husnain and Qureshy ( 1971 ) have studied several dikes from the southern peninsular shield of India. On the basis of paleomagnetic studies, some of the dikes have been found to be cor- relatable with the Deccan traps. From other countries there are examples of classification of dikes on the basis of paleomagnetic studi

tudies, some of the dikes have been found to be cor- relatable with the Deccan traps. From other countries there are examples of classification of dikes on the basis of paleomagnetic studies, such as Evans (1968) in Australia, Strangway (1965, 1966) and Larson and Strangway (1969) in Canada and the U.S.A. In this paper we report results of paleomagnetic studies of the Newer Dolerites from Singh- bhum, Rihar, India. During the Precambrian there appear to have been three main episodes of dike intru- sion throughout peninsular India (Pascoe 1950, p. 469). The earliest corresponded to the contcmporaneous traps of the Dharwar sys- tem. This was uniformly felt over the whole of peninsular India. The second episode is repre- sented by dikes and sills of the Cuddapah sys- tem. This was recognized mainly in many parts of the southern peninsula but more restrictedly in the northern half. The third one coincided with the outbursts of Malani rhyolites. This is more evident in the northern half of peninsula. The volcanic types of the Dharwar and those of Cuddapah are in most cases sharply con- trasted by the degree of alteration they exhibit. Can. J. Earth Sci., 11,1043-1054 (1974) CAN. J. EARTH SCI. Detailed formation names differ from locality to locality, but Har- rison (1972) has suggested a simplified nomen- clature for the entire Belt - Purcell Supergroup. In order to facilitate comparison with earlier work we have retained the older local nomen- clature (e.g., Price 1964) and have included Harrison's names in brackets where appropriate. Considerable radiometric data exist for Belt sediments, and a recent review, emphasizing current problems, has been given by Obradovich and Peterman (1973). The age of the formations sampled in this work assumes some importance when the geophysical implications of the paleo- magnetic results are considered. The relevant details are therefore discussed further below. At this point, it is sufficient to state that the entire Belt Supergroup probably represents a time interval as long as the Phanerozoic, being bracketed by ages of about 1700 m.y. and 800 m.y. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction Mississippi Valley-type ore deposits com- monly occur in relatively undisturbed host sediments that rest upon the continental base- ment and are therefore ideally suited to paleo- magnetic studies. In many cases it is possible to determine that the ore is younger than the enclosing sediments, but it is not possible by field and petrographic methods to determine how much younger. The common occurrence of anomalous leads means that radiometric age estimates based on galena may be mis- leading (e.g., Ohle 1959; Snyder and Gerde- mann 1968; Brown 1970). However, paleo- magnetic measurements appear to offer an alternative, independent check based upon ap- parent polar wandering curves. The disper- sion of directions is a measure of the individual departures from the applied field owing to anisotropy. Radiometric Evidence of Age The age of the basement rocks is not well defined. Biotites from the granitic rocks in the vicinity of the Nonacho basin gave K-Ar ages ranging from 1850 m.y. to 1735 m.y., musco- vites 2175 m.y. to 1745 m.y. (Wanless et al. 1963), and one hornblende 2240 m.y. (Bur- wash and Baadsgaard 1962). In the more gen- eral region south of Great Slave Lake and north of latitude 60°, K-Ar ages of micas range from 2555 m.y. to 1735 m.y., with most between 1900 and 1735 m.y. Both sedimentary and basement rocks are intruded by the Sparrow dikes. Fifty- four samples from 10 dikes have a stable magnetization with mean direction after a.f. cleaning of 131°, + 51" (N = 10, k = 50, a9, = 7") and a corresponding pole at 12" N, 069" W. The presence of reversals and the approximate agreement between dikes and their baked contracts are taken to indicate that the dikes were probably magnetized at the time of intrusion. 40Ar-39Ar studies suggest that the probable age of intrusion was about 1700 m.y. The magnetization of the Nonacho sedimentary rocks collected at 12 sites (40 samples) have a mean direction after thermal cleaning of 14g0,+57" (N = 12, k = 11, a9, = 14") without correction for geological dip. The corresponding pole is at 13' N, 086" W. The precision after correction for geological dip is low (k = 3), so the magnetization is predominantly post-folding. The precision after correction for geological dip is low (k = 3), so the magnetization is predominantly post-folding. The thermal decay characteristics and the geometry of the directions indicate that the magnetization of the sedimentary rocks was acquired during cooling following a period of mild heating presumably owing to deep burial. Minor syenite, nepheline syenite, and biotitic (in part vermiculite) rocks occur within the complex but their relationship to the ijolite suite and carbonatite is not clear because of the poor exposure. There is no petrographic evidence for metamorphism of the rock types and no apparent rotation of the intrusion since its emplacement. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction The carbonatite-alkalic rock complex near the 'elbow' in the Spanish River, Townships 107 and 108, Ontario, is a very poorly exposed elliptical intrusion into Archean granitic rocks. Trenching and drilling by Union Carbide Ex- ploration Co. (Fig. 1) have provided fresh material for magnetic and petrological studies. Much of the trenched material has weathered rapidly so that some digging was necessary to obtain fresh drill core for oriented samples. Sampling difficulties caused by weathering re- sulted in a small number of samples and large uncertainties in magnetization directions. Each group of trenches or outcrop was treated as a separate site, but within most sites, wide variations of rock type have yielded different magnetic characteristics and these have been treated as sub-sites (Fig. 1, Table 1). Drill cores were oriented in the field by suncompass using standard paleomagnetic tech- niques. Angles should be accurate to within two degrees. 'Contribution from the Earth Physics Branch No. 491. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction The carbonatite-alkalic rock complex near the 'elbow' in the Spanish River, Townships 107 and 108, Ontario, is a very poorly exposed elliptical intrusion into Archean granitic rocks. Trenching and drilling by Union Carbide Ex- ploration Co. (Fig. 1) have provided fresh material for magnetic and petrological studies. Much of the trenched material has weathered rapidly so that some digging was necessary to obtain fresh drill core for oriented samples. Sampling difficulties caused by weathering re- sulted in a small number of samples and large uncertainties in magnetization directions. Each group of trenches or outcrop was treated as a separate site, but within most sites, wide variations of rock type have yielded different magnetic characteristics and these have been treated as sub-sites (Fig. 1, Table 1). Drill cores were oriented in the field by suncompass using standard paleomagnetic tech- niques. Angles should be accurate to within two degrees. 'Contribution from the Earth Physics Branch No. 491. Geology and Age The Spanish River complex is composed of rocks of the ijolite suite and carbonatite in- truded into Archean granite and gneissic rocks. Minor syenite, nepheline syenite, and biotitic (in part vermiculite) rocks occur within the complex but their relationship to the ijolite suite and carbonatite is not clear because of the poor exposure. There is no petrographic evidence for metamorphism of the rock types and no apparent rotation of the intrusion since its emplacement. The complicated intermingling of rock types typical of carbonatite complexes is evident in a 1736 ft (529.5 m) hole collared at Site C and drilled into a magnetic anomaly by Union Carbide Exploration Co. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: 1973 Field observations and theoretical studies on temperate glaciers suggest that there is a layer of water at the icesediment interface. If this condition existed under continental glaciers it is reasonable to assume that rock and mineral particles were released from the base of the ice through a water or slurry medium. In order to test this hypothesis, samples of clay till from Port Alma, Ontario, were tested and shown to have a strong component of detrital remanent magnetization (DRM) which resists alternating field demag- netization. The possibility that the remanence alignment was caused by glacier movement has been ruled out by anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility measurements. Thus the results demonstrate that a water or slurry layer existed at the base of continental glaciers at the time of till deposition. The basal water layer may explain the very rapid advance of the glacier lobes through the basins of the Great Lakes. The paleomagnetic data and available radiocarbon dates suggest that the till at Port Alma was deposited in a relatively short period of about 100 to 400 yr. The potential usefulness of DRM in clay-rich tills for strati- graphic studies is being further investigated. Discussion of Remanence Results The within-block variations in RM, directions are small, resulting in RM, directions with high k and low values. Thus the Port Stanley Till exhibits a statistically significant variation in RM, directions at different elevations in the section. It is therefore deduced for the Port Stanley Till that material was released from the base of the ice by melting so that the particles were deposited from a water slurry, thereby allowing the magnetite particles to rotate into alignment with the earth's magnetic field to form a detrital remanent magnetization (DRM) in the till. The variations in declination and inclination are shown in Figs. 4 and 5. They exhibit a 'cyclic' behavior for approximately every 125 cm of till section, during which the declination oscillates about 30" and the inclination about 15 ". When the virtual geomagnetic poles (VGP) calculated from the RM, directions using the dipole hypothesis for these till blocks are ex- amined (Fig. 6), it is apparent that they cluster in north-central Russia. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction The Topley Intrusions outcrop in a NW-SE trending belt some 150 mi (240 km) long by 40 mi (64 km) wide, which is centered near the town of Endako in central British Columbia (Fig. 1). The name, Topley Intrusions, refers to a number of composite felsic batholiths and stocks that intrude tectonically stable rock of the northern Interior Plateau. With few excep tions these intrusions show no petrographic evi- dence of secondary alteration or internal de- formation. In the Endako area they have been geologically mapped and radiometrically dated in considerable detail. These features led to their selection for paleomagnetic study to de- termine whether the various intrusive phases could be classified by remanence direction as has been possible with similar rocks elsewhere (Symons 1972b). section_candidates.excerpt: rocks of the Seal and Croteau were formed in the interval (~1200 to 2.1500 m.y. ago) during which time the paleomagnetic pole (relative to the Precambrian Shield of North America) was previously thought to have remained al- most stationary near the present-day equator (Palmer 1969, Spall 1971 ). Geology The Croteau and Seal Groups form an elon- gate belt of volcanic and sedimentary rocks that is preserved chiefly adjacent to, and north of the Grenville Front in Labrador (Fig. 1). The Croteau as defined (Fahrig 1959) consists of two parts, the lower being made up of black pyritic shales, graywacke, quartzite, dolomite, and metabasalt. This is overlain unconformably along Croteau and Pocket Knife Lakes by a basal conglomerate followed by sandstones. The latter is feldspathic and consists of alter- nating pink, maroon, and cream colored layers. Coarser phases of the sandstone are cross bedded and locally have a carbonate cement. The sandstones may be partly tuffaceous as devitrified shards are locally abundant. Above this basal zone the Croteau Group consists largely of intermediate to acid, purplish to green volcanic porphyries with thin layers of cross-bedded, tuffaceous cream to purple sand- stone. In the present report the name Croteau will be restricted to the predominantly volcanic se- quence that lies above the unconformity. The Croteau Group thus defined, is Helikian in age, whereas the rocks below the unconformity may be significantly older, perhaps Aphebian in age. In the Snegamook Lake map area (Fahrig 1957, 1959, Brummer and Mann 1961) the strataform rocks of the Seal Group fall into five major lithostratigraphic units. The pre- dominant rock types of the five units, proceed- ing from the base of the group upward, are: (1) shales and coarse clastics, (2) volcanics and sandstones, (3) diabase with interlayered sandstone and shale, (4) volcanics and shale, and (5) sandstone. The presence of two separate volcanic sequences suggests cyclicity of igneous activity; however, the sedimentary rocks between the two volcanic sequences are extensively intruded by gabbro and diabase sills. It is conceivable that these intrusions are evidence of continuing igneous activity in the interval between the two periods of volcanism. Geology The Croteau and Seal Groups form an elon- gate belt of volcanic and sedimentary rocks that is preserved chiefly adjacent to, and north of the Grenville Front in Labrador (Fig. 1). The Croteau as defined (Fahrig 1959) consists of two parts, the lower being made up of black pyritic shales, graywacke, quartzite, dolomite, and metabasalt. This is overlain unconformably along Croteau and Pocket Knife Lakes by a basal conglomerate followed by sandstones. The latter is feldspathic and consists of alter- nating pink, maroon, and cream colored layers. Coarser phases of the sandstone are cross bedded and locally have a carbonate cement. The sandstones may be partly tuffaceous as devitrified shards are locally abundant. Above this basal zone the Croteau Group consists largely of intermediate to acid, purplish to green volcanic porphyries with thin layers of cross-bedded, tuffaceous cream to purple sand- stone. In the present report the name Croteau will be restricted to the predominantly volcanic se- quence that lies above the unconformity. The Croteau Group thus defined, is Helikian in age, whereas the rocks below the unconformity may be significantly older, perhaps Aphebian in age. In the Snegamook Lake map area (Fahrig 1957, 1959, Brummer and Mann 1961) the strataform rocks of the Seal Group fall into five major lithostratigraphic units. The pre- dominant rock types of the five units, proceed- ing from the base of the group upward, are: (1) shales and coarse clastics, (2) volcanics and sandstones, (3) diabase with interlayered sandstone and shale, (4) volcanics and shale, and (5) sandstone. The presence of two separate volcanic sequences suggests cyclicity of igneous activity; however, the sedimentary rocks between the two volcanic sequences are extensively intruded by gabbro and diabase sills. It is conceivable that these intrusions are evidence of continuing igneous activity in the interval between the two periods of volcanism. The presence of two separate volcanic sequences suggests cyclicity of igneous activity; however, the sedimentary rocks between the two volcanic sequences are extensively intruded by gabbro and diabase sills. It is conceivable that these intrusions are evidence of continuing igneous activity in the interval between the two periods of volcanism. The sedimentary rocks of the Seal Group exhibit an oscillatory but steady upward fining from the base of the group to the base of the uppermost preserved unit which is sandstone. The stronger of these is directed at a moderate angle to the southeast; the weaker at a shallow angle to the west. This is overlain unconformably along Croteau and Pocket Knife Lakes by a basal conglomerate followed by sandstones. The latter is feldspathic and consists of alter- nating pink, maroon, and cream colored layers. Coarser phases of the sandstone are cross bedded and locally have a carbonate cement. The sandstones may be partly tuffaceous as devitrified shards are locally abundant. Methods Samples were collected from a total of 23 sites, 13 of which were situated in sediments and 10 in igneous rocks. At each of the sedi- mentary sites 3 or 4 hand samples were col- lected, yielding a total of 40 blocks. The igneous samples were collected by both field- drilling (36 cores) and hand-sampling (1 3 blocks). Most samples were oriented using a sun-compass. Due to overcast conditions some sedimentary samples were oriented magnetically. Comparison of magnetic and solar bearings, where possible, indicates that orientation errors do not exceed 5 " . All measurements of remanence were made on a commercial spinner magnetometer and routine partial demagnetization studies have been carried out on all specimens used in the final analysis. Alternating field (a.f. ) demag- netization was performed with an apparatus closely similar to that described by McElhinny ( 1966). Thermal cleaning experiments em- ployed a small furnace located in a room-sized magnetic shield similar to that described by Patton and Fitch (1962); the magnetic field over the volume occupied by the specimens is not more than 5y. The procedure adopted involves step-wise partial demagnetization (by both methods) of one pilot specimen per sample and analysis of the results in terms of within-site scatter. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: te stable magnetization. The flows form two groups of normally magnetized (N) flows, each overlying reversely magnetized (R) flows. It is suggested that the sequence consists of a single sequence of R flows overlain by N flows, the sequence being repeated by faulting. A mean pole position calculated from 15 N sites is 30" N, 183" E, (dp = 5, dm = 8), and the pole position from 12 R sites is 49" N, 232" E (dp = 14, dm = 16). Reasons are given for believing that this difference in pole position between the older (R) and younger (N) flows was caused by relative movement of the Keweenawan area and the rotation axis of the earth, and not to secondary components of magnetization acquired since the rocks cooled. Review of the Keweenawan paleomagnetic data reveals a consistent picture of an older reversely magnetized and younger normally magnetized magnetic field (if allowance is made for radiogenic errors). The time at which the field switched from reversed to normal polarity may provide a valuable time datum traceable in the rocks from continent to continent. The flows form two groups of normally magnetized (N) flows, each overlying reversely magnetized (R) flows. It is suggested that the sequence consists of a single sequence of R flows overlain by N flows, the sequence being repeated by faulting. Statement of Objectives The first task in paleomagnetic work is to survey the directions of magnetization. The second is to determine when, during the history of the rock, the directions were acquired. Since the Et-Then sediments have been extensively intruded by diabase it is necessary to determine to what extent they have been remagnetized during the period of heating associated with these intrusions. It is useful also to determine the time at which the diabases themselves be- came magnetized. The answers to these ques- tions can be obtained by making use of the classical igneous contact test (work of David reviewed in Bruhnes 1906, Irving 1964, Everitt and Clegg 1962). Therefore a study of the diabase, of unaltered Et-Then sediments, and of the Et-Then sediments baked by the diabase has been made. Within the Fold Belt a succession of folded 'Earth Physics Branch contribution no. 384. sedimentary and volcanic rocks of the Great Slave Supergroup (Aphebian) overlies a base- ment of granitoid gneisses which yield Archean radiometric ages (Table 1). Dioritic and syeni- tic bodies, that yield three K-Ar biotite ages of 1630, 1795, and 1845 m.y. (Lowdon et al. 1963; Wanless et al. 1970), intrude the lower part of the Great Slave strata. The Et-Then Group unconformably overlies the Great Slave Supergroup. It is a gently- dipping sequence of fluviatile sediments about 5000 m thick, and is divided into the Murky Formation beneath and the Preble Formation above. The Murky consists of massive con- glomerates separated by thin lenses of red shale, siltstone, and sandstone. The Preble is composed for the most part of red or buff lithic and feldspathic sandstones. It attains a thickness of about 3000 m. Sedimentological studies of the conglomerates indicate that the transport direction was from south-east to north-west (Hoffman 1969). Statement of Objectives The first task in paleomagnetic work is to survey the directions of magnetization. The second is to determine when, during the history of the rock, the directions were acquired. Since the Et-Then sediments have been extensively intruded by diabase it is necessary to determine to what extent they have been remagnetized during the period of heating associated with these intrusions. It is useful also to determine the time at which the diabases themselves be- came magnetized. The answers to these ques- tions can be obtained by making use of the classical igneous contact test (work of David reviewed in Bruhnes 1906, Irving 1964, Everitt and Clegg 1962). Therefore a study of the diabase, of unaltered Et-Then sediments, and of the Et-Then sediments baked by the diabase has been made. Within the Fold Belt a succession of folded 'Earth Physics Branch contribution no. 384. sedimentary and volcanic rocks of the Great Slave Supergroup (Aphebian) overlies a base- ment of granitoid gneisses which yield Archean radiometric ages (Table 1). Dioritic and syeni- tic bodies, that yield three K-Ar biotite ages of 1630, 1795, and 1845 m.y. (Lowdon et al. 1963; Wanless et al. 1970), intrude the lower part of the Great Slave strata. The Et-Then Group unconformably overlies the Great Slave Supergroup. It is a gently- dipping sequence of fluviatile sediments about 5000 m thick, and is divided into the Murky Formation beneath and the Preble Formation above. The Murky consists of massive con- glomerates separated by thin lenses of red shale, siltstone, and sandstone. The Preble is composed for the most part of red or buff lithic and feldspathic sandstones. It attains a thickness of about 3000 m. Sedimentological studies of the conglomerates indicate that the transport direction was from south-east to north-west (Hoffman 1969). Statement of Objectives The first task in paleomagnetic work is to survey the directions of magnetization. The second is to determine when, during the history of the rock, the directions were acquired. Since the Et-Then sediments have been extensively intruded by diabase it is necessary to determine to what extent they have been remagnetized during the period of heating associated with these intrusions. It is useful also to determine the time at which the diabases themselves be- came magnetized. The answers to these ques- tions can be obtained by making use of the classical igneous contact test (work of David reviewed in Bruhnes 1906, Irving 1964, Everitt and Clegg 1962). Therefore a study of the diabase, of unaltered Et-Then sediments, and of the Et-Then sediments baked by the diabase has been made. Methods Generally, about 5 oriented cores, 2.5 cm in diameter, have been obtained from each site. Where the rock was hard usually 2 or 3 hand samples have been collected. The site numbers (Fig. 1 ) are arbitrary and have no stratigraphic significance. Measurements of intensity and di- rection of magnetization have been made using a commercial spinner magnetometer. Geology The rocks studied occur in the east arm of the Great Slave Lake (Fig. 1). The region is part of the East Arm Fold Belt which is a subprovince of the Churchill Structural Prov- ince (Stockwell 1964). It is bounded on the south-east by the McDonald fault system and on the north by the Archean Slave Province. Within the Fold Belt a succession of folded 'Earth Physics Branch contribution no. 384. sedimentary and volcanic rocks of the Great Slave Supergroup (Aphebian) overlies a base- ment of granitoid gneisses which yield Archean radiometric ages (Table 1). Dioritic and syeni- tic bodies, that yield three K-Ar biotite ages of 1630, 1795, and 1845 m.y. (Lowdon et al. 1963; Wanless et al. 1970), intrude the lower part of the Great Slave strata. The Et-Then Group unconformably overlies the Great Slave Supergroup. It is a gently- dipping sequence of fluviatile sediments about 5000 m thick, and is divided into the Murky Formation beneath and the Preble Formation above. The re- sults reported herein and those recently ob- tained from the Et-Then Group and the Dubawnt Group indicate that the pole then (proceeding backwards in time) moved east- wards in a broad sweep to the vicinity of what is nowadays northern South America. Results from oldest Proterozoic (Aphebian) and Archean rocks are scanty, but they can be connected by a return loop into the southeast Pacific as shown in Fig. 12. These results, to- gether with those already published for younger Proterozoic rocks (the polar path is given in Fig. 12) indicate that during the Proterozoic, the path of apparent polar wandering relative to the Canadian Shield made several loops, with peak-to-peak amplitudes of approximately 90' and periods of several hundred million years. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: y. 1. Introduction Palaeomagnetic data for Sicily are lacking except for very young rocks. To facilitate palaeomagnetic comparisons with the Mediterranean area and the adjacent plates a palaeomagnetic survey of Sicily has been carried out. First results from volcanic rocks of Upper Cretaceous age are reported in this paper. 2. Geology The volcanic formation investigated lies in the extreme Southeast of Sicily at Capo Passero (fig. 1). The rocks which were formed by submarine eruptions consist of compact lava intermixed in some cases with pillows. Into the basaltic mass many dikes were in- truded, According to Colacicchi [1] the petrographic composition of the igneous material may be classified as a tephritic magma. The volcanic rocks are overlaid conformally by limestones which are well dated by the aid of fossils as Maestrichtian (Uppermost Creta- ceous) [1]. As the deposition of the limestone began shortly after the end of the submarine ejections [1] an Uppermost Cretaceous age (about 70-80 my) can be attributed to the lavas. Due to several tectonic movements in the Tertiary the igneous rocks were uplifted. A small amount of tilting of the volcanic rocks may be possible but only 2 ° or less inclining SSE [ 1; Rittmann, private commu- nication]. Because of its u

g the Creta- ceous (e.g. Pitman et al. [6]), pole positions of Upper and Lower Cretaceous should be distinguished. The Lower Cretaceous pole for Africa according to Briden [7] (60.5°N 260.5°E) is significantly different from the Upper Cretaceous pole (63.5°N, 218°E) given by E1 Shazly and Krs [8]. This pole coincides well with that of Sicily for the Upper Cretaceous (see fig. 3). It is therefore concluded that no large relative motion of Sicily with respect to Africa has occurred at least since the Upper Cretaceous. This is consistent with the suggestion that Sicily is an eastern prolongation of the North African continent (e.g. Caire [9]). The Strait of Sicily seems to be a submerged part of the African con- tinent joining Sicily to North Africa. The motion of Sicily since the Upper Cretaceous is probably similar to that of Africa with respect to Europe. Following the reconstruction of Pitman et al. [6] the general movement of Africa with respect to "stable" Europe from 80 my to the present is west- ward (and northward) associated with a counter-clock- wise rotation in the order of 20 ° about a pole in Tangier. This is in agreement with the significant diffe- rence of the present day positions of the (Upper) Cretaceous pole positions for Africa and Sicily on

From each site about 6 diffe- rent cores (2.5 cm diameter) were collected. A total of 19 sites (107 cores) were sampled. The remanent magnetization was measured with a fluxgate spinner magnetometer. One pilot speci- men from each site was chosen for stepwise demag- netization in alternating magnetic fields using a peak value op to 500 Oe. Most samples carried an unsta- ble component of remanence which disappeared in fields ranging between 100 and 300 Oe for the diffe- rent sites. All remaining samples were then treated in the appropriate alternating fields. This paper de- scribes the results of a recent study made on a basic plutonic intrusion in southeast Morocco, dated on the basis of stratigraphic evidence as Famenlan (Upper Devonian) (HoUard, personal commumcation, 1969). A further four sites (4, 5, 20, 21) were collected from Cenomanian white limestones at Illasi and Valdobbia. dene and two sites (6, 14) from Tertiary basalts. Most of the sites exhibit magnetic stability on thermal demagnetisation (Fig. 2) and only three sites (23-25) were rejected due to poor stability. The deposit has a maximum thick- ness of 2.5 m and was again principally pisolitic with reworked bauxite intraclasts. The nature of the mate- rial is more consistent throughout its thickness than that at San Giovanni Rotondo. Twelve of the sites were from bauxites, the other site (30) came from the overlying Senonian limestone, but this was too weakly magnetic for precise measurement. Two sites (17, 18) from the Jurassic "Ammonitico Rosso" formation near Asiago were found to be unstable. Most of the sites exhibit magnetic stability on thermal demagnetisation (Fig. 2) and only three sites (23-25) were rejected due to poor stability. Site 10 was rejected due to its poor within-site group- ing and site 20 was too weakly magnetic for precise measurement. Sites 6, 14 and 15 are basalts of uncer- tain age, probably Tertiary, and cannot be considered for the ascertation of the Cretaceous directions (Table 2, Fig. 3). The concordance of the results from these three regions bears out the assumption that little rotation has occurred between the different units and that the mean result can be used to ascer- tain the rotation of the southern Dolomites relative to Europe and Africa. 4. Northern Apennines The Umbrian sequence of the Apennines (Fig. 1) is considered autochthonous or para-autochthonous [21] and also contains a highly magnetically stable horizon. The scaglia horizon of the Umbrian sequence has a total thickness of 210-470 m [22] and com- prises fine-grained deep-water marly limestones which are red, white or, rarely, green in colour. The Scaglia outcrops sporadically along a zone 60 km wide which runs from Urbino in the north to Rieti in the south, a distance of some 200 km. Renz [23,24] distinguished four biozones within the Scaglia which range in age from Cenomanian to Early Eocene. The principal zone that was sampled was the Scaglia Rossa which was originally given an age of Turonian - Campanian [23,24], but is now considered to extend into the Palaeocene [22]. Nonetheless, Permian and Triassic results from the southern Alps [4,7] when compared with results from stable Europe differ by 50 ° in declination. This has been widely accepted to indicate a post-Late Triassic 50 ° anti- clockwise rotation, relative to Europe, of an Italian "microplate". Soffel [6] has suggested that most or all of this rotation occurred between the Late Eocene and Late Miocene, based on palaeomagnetic work from Colli Euganei in the southern Dolomites. The scaglia horizon of the Umbrian sequence has a total thickness of 210-470 m [22] and com- prises fine-grained deep-water marly limestones which are red, white or, rarely, green in colour. The means of the 27 Upper Cretaceous/Palaeocene sites were well grouped (k = i9.0, a95 = 6.5) but there was a marked spread in declination. Part of this spread could be due to tectonic rotations occurring during the age range of the samples, bu the mean of the magnetic directions should nevertheless give a good representa- tion of the magnetic direction pertaining to the Latest Cretaceous and Early Palaeocene. uenced by faulting, there are no indications of large-scale allochthonous movement. The main horizon sampled is similar in age and lithology to that sampled from the Umbrian sequence and comprises the Senonian Red Scaglia from which 17 sites were collected from three locali- ties - Illasi (Verona), Schio and Valdobbiadene. A further four sites (4, 5, 20, 21) were collected from Cenomanian white limestones at Illasi and Valdobbia. dene and two sites (6, 14) from Tertiary basalts. Two sites (17, 18) from the Jurassic "Ammonitico Rosso" formation near Asiago were found to be unstable. Most of the sites exhibit magnetic stability on thermal demagnetisation (Fig. 2) and only three sites (23-25) were rejected due to poor stability. Site 10 was rejected due to its poor within-site group- ing and site 20 was too weakly magnetic for precise measurement. Sites 6, 14 and 15 are basalts of uncer- tain age, probably Tertiary, and cannot be considered for the ascertation of the Cretaceous directions (Table 2, Fig. 3). The concordance of the results from these three regions bears out the assumption that little rotation has occurred between the different units and that the mean result can be used to ascer- tain the rotation of the southern Dolomites relative to Europe and Africa. 4. The deviation of the pole associated with the Campania platform from the African polar wandering curve is probably due to the allochthonous nature of this unit. The deviation of the Umbrian sequence pole may also be due to allochthony [22], but it is also possible that the Umbrian sequence rotated by 15 °, relative to the Dolomites and Apulia, due to de- coupling of the northern Apennine "autochthon" from the rest of autochthonous Italy along the Anzio- Ancona line and beneath the Po Basin. Introduction In a review of Mediterranean palaeomagnetic data, Zijderveld and Van der Voo [1] discuss the systematic deviations between palaeomagnetic data from land- masses and peninsulas of Mediterranean Europe and those from "Stable Europe". These "Tethys" direc- tions proved to fit reasonably well with the African palaeomagnetic pattern. This led them to the tentative conclusion that the landmasses south of the Pyrenean -Alpine mountain belt (i.e. Iberian Peninsula, Sardinia, Corsica, Italy including the Southern Alps) belonged to the African plate. Introduction In a review of Mediterranean palaeomagnetic data, Zijderveld and Van der Voo [1] discuss the systematic deviations between palaeomagnetic data from land- masses and peninsulas of Mediterranean Europe and those from "Stable Europe". These "Tethys" direc- tions proved to fit reasonably well with the African palaeomagnetic pattern. This led them to the tentative conclusion that the landmasses south of the Pyrenean -Alpine mountain belt (i.e. Iberian Peninsula, Sardinia, Corsica, Italy including the Southern Alps) belonged to the African plate. A rotation of these landmasses as part of the African plate implies synchroneity in rotation. Other volcanics, including trachytes, ignim- brites of different compositions, andesites and basalts, occurring in flows, domes, dykes and small plateaus, were formed between the Oligo-Miocene and the Pleistocene in different areas of the graben. A sketch map of the Tertiary volcanics associated with the Campidano and other grabens of Sardinia is shown in Fig. 1 [5]. 2. Laboratory tests and results Paleomagnetic data from fourteen sampling sites in the Tertiary volcanics are reported here; the exact geo- graphical locations are given in the Appendix together with short petrographic descriptions. The suggested age of most of the volcanics sampled is Miocene and possibly Pliocene (basalts which are commonly assigned to the latest Plio-Pleistocene volcanic activity have not been sampled); however, no comprehensive petrological or even geological study of these volcanites has yet been published although the rock types have been referred to as basalts, andesites, andesitic porphyries, trachytes, rhyolites and acidic ignimbrites. The petro- logic variation within the collection is remarkable but all seem to be related to the genesis of the graben. From the fourteen numbered sampling sites (Fig. 1) 69 oriented h

ction A of Fig. 6 includes all Tertiary sites, and the direction B excludes sites with paleode- clinations comprised between 35 ° and 10 °. At a few outcrops differently oriented declinations, to the northeast and to the west, were found [17,19,20] Inclinations vary remarkably. It would appear that speculation on the form of the past geomagnetic field in Sardinia is not justified on the basis of these scanty and deviating data, and that their possible tectonic significance still needs an accurate assessment. 5. Conclusion The new paleomagnetic data from Campidano are in good agreement with most Tertiary data for Sardinia and reinforce the general picture of "African" direc- tions of the past geomagnetic field. Improved knowl- edge of the ages of the volcanics of the Campidano and its associated grabens would certainly help to establish the age of the transition of the paleomagnetic declina- tions from the northwest to the north and hence the age of significant geodynamic activity in the western Mediterranean Sea. Received 19 September 1972 Revised version received 1 December 1972 The paleomagnetism of the Late Cretaceous Polos de Caldas alkaline complex (46.6°W, 21.9°S) was investigated through 42 oriented cores from seven sites. Six sites, reversed relative to the present magnetic field of the Earth, yield a pole at 127°W, 82°S (dp= 8 °, dm= 13°). This pole is located close to other Late Cretaceous poles for South America obtained by Creer [1] from untreated paleomagnetic samples. The results are significantly different from those for the nearby Early Cretaceous Serra Geral basalt but close to the Triassic pole for South America. The polar wandering path for South America for the Mesozoic seems to be more complicated than anticipated. The available paleomagnetic information may not yet be precise enough to determine the time of opening of the Atlantic. 1. In

Introduction Paleomagnetism of Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks of South America and Africa probably records the opening of the South Atlantic. Unless such opening was through a rotation about a pole close to the axis of rotation of the Earth, the time of this tectonic phenomenon should be recorded by a fork in the superimposed polar wandering curves of South America and Africa. This report presents new paleomagnetic information on the Late Cretaceous of South America and evaluates it in relation to other available data. Oriented cores were taken with the assistance of I. The natural remanence of 29 samples obtained from relatively fresh rock in two localities was found to consist of two components with overlapping coercivity ranges. Alternating field treatment proved ineffective for removing the secondary component without destroying the primary one. Thermal demagneti- zation of samples from the two localities was more effective and yielded paleomagnetic poles at 14.7 ° N, 11.6°W and 58.9 ° N, 15.9°E respectively. These pole positions are different from those available from contemporaneous North American rocks and from poles derived from Jamaican Cretaceous and Upper Miocene rocks. different from those available from contemporaneous North American rocks and from poles derived from Jamaican Cretaceous and Upper Miocene rocks. Mineralogical studies showed that the granodiorite has undergone an extensive maghemitization superposed on earlier class 2 deuteric oxidation and related to the weathering process. Some of the titanomaghemite has, however, been converted to titanohematite. Hence although the secondary remanence carried by the former was removable by thermal treat- ment at 500°C, its part carried by the latter could not be removed without simultaneously destroying the primary remanence carried by the residual titanomagnetite. The observed paleopole positions do not, therefore, represent the true Paleocene geomagnetic field, but suggest that the direction of magnetization of the pluton has been approx- imately equatorial and was probably acquired in a reversed geomagnetic field. This could be interpreted as having been caused by the behavior of the geomagnetic field during a polarity transition, but a more favorable interpretation appears to be a large anticlockwise tectonic rotation of the islands since the Paleocene. 1. Turner [ 11 ] has described a natural process whereby the decomposition products of ferromagnesian minerals eventually break down into magnetite when heated in an oxidizing atmosphere. It would appear that in the present case a similar effect has taken place in the laboratory and that heat treatment has "generated" some magnetite from the decomposition products of the ferromagnesian minerals already present in the rocks. It was emplaced in the Early Tertiary as a solid intrusion, but probably was above its Curie temperature at the time and so became magnetized substantially in situ. If so, it must have undergone considerable tectonic disturbance subsequent to emplacement and magnetization, including an important component of clockwise rotation. Examination of paleomagnetic data for the westernmost Cordillera shows that an abnormal number of rock bodies have discordant directions of remanent magnetization, mostly clockwise rotations of declina- tion, flattened inclinations, or both. Internally the intrusion exhibits several superimposed stages of solid-state deformation, char- acterized by crystallographic orientation of olivine grains, folding and displacement of mineral bands, cleavage, cataclasis, and the like. Ragan [1 ], who describes these structures in detail, believes that they developed at temperatures of 500°C or a few hundred degrees higher. The intrusion is believed by most in- vestigators to have been emplaced in the solid-state at a temperature well below the solidus. However, Ragan's estimates of temperature and the paleomagnetic evi- dence cited below suggest that it was above its Curie temperature when emplaced and thus acquired its magnetization substantially it situ. Fig. 1 (insert) is a simplified version of a geological map of the northern Cascade Range by Misch [4], showing the complicated regional setting of the Twin Sisters Intrusion. Introduction The Twin Sisters Intrusion of northwestern Wash- ington is well known to petrologists and geochemists as a source of nearly pure, unaltered dunite for lab- oratory experiments, where it is often cast in the role of a sample of the earth's mantle. According to Ragan [1 ], it consists essentially of four minerals, olivine (Fo90 or more), enstatite, chromite, and clinopyrox- ene, with olivine greatly predominant. Unlike most Alpine ultramafic bodies, the Twin Sisters Intrusion is almost completely unserpentinized except at its margin [1], although a model calculated by Thomp- son [2] from gravity and aeromagnetic data indicates the presence of a greater amount of serpentine at depth. Unlike most Alpine ultramafic bodies, the Twin Sisters Intrusion is almost completely unserpentinized except at its margin [1], although a model calculated by Thomp- son [2] from gravity and aeromagnetic data indicates the presence of a greater amount of serpentine at depth. Gravity and magnetic measurements also show that the intrusion is relatively thin and lens shaped, with a maximum vertical dimension of a few kilom- eters [2,3]. Internally the intrusion exhibits several superimposed stages of solid-state deformation, char- acterized by crystallographic orientation of olivine grains, folding and displacement of mineral bands, cleavage, cataclasis, and the like. Ragan [1 ], who describes these structures in detail, believes that they developed at temperatures of 500°C or a few hundred degrees higher. The intrusion is believed by most in- vestigators to have been emplaced in the solid-state at a temperature well below the solidus. However, Ragan's estimates of temperature and the paleomagnetic evi- dence cited below suggest that it was above its Curie temperature when emplaced and thus acquired its magnetization substantially it situ. [1] have described the island's geomor- phology and the geochemistry which suggests an early stage of evolution from a tholeiitic to an akaline vol- cano. The paleomagnetic data have been published [2] providing evidence for at least two excursions of the magnetic field during the Brunhes epoch (t = 0-0.69 m.y.), and values for the angular dispersion of virtual geomagnetic poles (VGP) consistent with the present average behaviour of the geomagnetic field in the same latitudes. Methods Field. Up to eight separate cores of 2.5 cm diame- ter and average length 12 cm were drilled from each of 15 separate lava and 3 minor intrusive bodies on the island, using a gasoline-powered portable drill. Spacing between cores in each body averaged 5 m. Samples were oriented in geographic coordinates to a precision of-+2.5 ° while still attached to outcrop. Directions of remanent magnetism be- fore and after treatment in peak alternating magnetic fields of 100 and 200 oersteds were measured using a spinner magnetometer. Samples were selected for K/At dating using two criteria: the bodies involved should be in known strati- graphic sequence, and the samples should be fresh and unaltered. The sedimentary episode during which the Embalse Rio Tercero Formation was formed, was interrupted by a volcanic cycle. During this cycle more than seven lava flows were formed; sediments which were laid down between the lava flows have the same charac- teristics as those formed before the volcanic cycle [6]. The Vulcanitas Cerro Colorado Formation include the lava flows extruded in this first volcanic cycle and their interbedded continental sediments. Rocks of this formation are fairly well exposed in the Cerro Colo- rado area, about 32 ° South, 64 ° West.
